strengths: Clearly identifies and articulates the concrete problem of sequence length mismatch between speech and text tokens in joint speech-text modeling
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation including quality metrics (WER, UTMOS), similarity metrics (speaker/emotion/duration consistency), and two established benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze)
Achieves significant practical benefits: 10× bitrate reduction compared to SpeechTokenizer and enables effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) with small models
End-to-end approach that learns text-aligned tokenization without explicit word-level supervision during core training
Competitive performance on StoryCloze semantic evaluation despite using smaller models and fewer trainable parameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (Transformer encoder-aggregator, RVQ quantization, cross-entropy loss) are standard; the contribution is primarily in their combination

Critical absence of ablation studies: no ablations on modified cross-attention mechanism, choice of shallow representations as keys, aggregator design, RVQ parameters, or Distil-Whisper initialization

Unfair experimental comparisons: text-only baseline lacks speech features (fundamentally different), different model sizes across comparisons, and initialization from Distil-Whisper/CosyVoice provides unexplored advantages

Unsubstantiated claims: computational efficiency claimed but no timing/throughput/memory comparisons provided; paralinguistic information preservation claimed but duration consistency (0.73) is notably worse than S3 token (0.83); UTMOS exceeds ground truth (suspicious)
Acoustic performance not state-of-the-art on SALMON: Spirit LM Expr. achieves 73.5% sentiment accuracy vs. TASTE's 59.0%

ASR dependency under-explored: no analysis of sensitivity to ASR errors, evaluation only on English, and claims of 'no word-level alignment required' misleading given Section 3.2's word-level processing
Limited scope: evaluation only on English datasets, only two benchmarks used, no human evaluation or listening tests, no generated speech samples shown
Algorithm 1 for vocabulary mismatch is ad-hoc and lacks justification for why word-level grouping/averaging is the correct approach
Notation clarity issues with multiple overlapping length variables; missing technical details on word boundary determination during training

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifies the genuine challenge of speech-text token length mismatch in joint SLM modeling
Impressive tokenization efficiency: Achieves ~10x lower bitrate (~190 bits) compared to SpeechTokenizer while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality (UTMOS 4.25)
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: Provides both quality assessment (WER, UTMOS) and similarity metrics (speaker, emotion, duration consistency) for reconstruction
End-to-end learning without explicit alignment: Automatically learns text-aligned tokenization through reconstruction objective without requiring manual word-level alignments
Practical system design: Enables straightforward parameter-efficient adaptation of text LLMs to SLMs using LoRA fine-tuning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (ASR initialization, cross-attention, RVQ quantization, reconstruction objectives) are well-established; the main contribution (using shallow hidden in cross-attention) is a minor modification

Unclear differentiation from CosyVoice [6]: The paper heavily relies on CosyVoice's S3 tokens and acknowledges prior exploration of shallow representations. Claims of being 'first' are not well-justified
Missing critical ablations: No ablations on ASR initialization impact, shallow vs. last hidden comparison, RVQ hyperparameter sensitivity, or word-level averaging contribution
Weak baseline performance: S3 token baseline + LoRA performs surprisingly poorly on StoryCloze (63.0), suggesting implementation issues that undermine baseline credibility

Inconsistent SLM evaluation: TASLM (59.0 sentiment, 68.0 speaker) does not clearly outperform prior work (TWIST: 61.5/69.0; Spirit LM Expr.: 73.5/81.0), and comparisons mix different experimental settings
Ad-hoc vocabulary mismatch solution: Algorithm 1's word-level grouping/averaging/alignment lacks principled justification; no robustness analysis to ASR errors in word boundaries
Problematic bitrate evaluation: Acknowledged as 'estimation rather than fixed number' due to dynamic compression, undermining quantitative comparison with fixed-rate methods
Duration consistency gap unexplored: TASTE achieves 0.73 vs. 0.88 for SpeechTokenizer; dynamic compression explanation insufficient without deeper investigation
Limited evaluation scope: Only LibriTTS test-clean (reading style); no cross-domain evaluation despite Emilia dataset use; qualitative analysis and failure cases absent

Reproducibility and dependency concerns: Heavy reliance on external models (Distil-Whisper, CosyVoice, HifiGAN) with unclear modifications; no code release statement; multiple unjustified hyperparameters

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing real modality gap in speech-text joint modeling
Impressive compression results: 10x lower bitrate (~190) vs SpeechTokenizer (~2000) while maintaining comparable quality (UTMOS 4.25)
Elegant end-to-end design without explicit word-level alignments during training
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: quality, similarity, and downstream SLM benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze)
Clear practical contribution enabling parameter-efficient LLM-to-SLM adaptation via LoRA
Strong speech reconstruction quality with UTMOS scores surpassing ground truth
Well-written with informative figures and clear methodology presentation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (Transformer aggregator, RVQ, ASR initialization) with new motivation rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Critical unaddressed dependence on ASR quality: no evaluation of robustness to ASR errors, generalization to other ASR systems, or applicability to low-resource languages
Ad-hoc vocabulary mismatch solution (Algorithm 1): word-level averaging loses information without principled justification; no ablation study on this critical component
Notable performance gaps on downstream tasks: Spirit LM Expr. (73.5 vs 59.0 on SALMON sentiment) and ASR+LLM (95.9 vs 89.5 on StoryCloze) substantially outperform TASLM without adequate explanation
Insufficient ablation studies: no investigation of aggregator design choices, word-level averaging, quantization depth sensitivity, or RVQ layer justification

Missing computational analysis: no inference speed comparison, training/inference cost analysis, or STE gradient flow investigation

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: effectively identifies the length-mismatch challenge in joint speech-text modeling and proposes an intuitive solution using text-aligned tokenization

Comprehensive evaluation: extensive metrics across reconstruction quality, similarity, and SLM performance; includes human evaluation, standard benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and multiple evaluation dimensions

Strong empirical results: achieves extremely low bitrate (~150 bps) while maintaining competitive quality; speech continuation shows clear improvements over baselines; importantly, preserves text LLM capabilities

Well-designed attention mechanism: cross-attention aggregation is elegant and well-justified; clear intuition for using text queries, last hidden states for alignment, and shallow representations for reconstruction

Practical applicability: demonstrates text-aligned speech editing, showing the representations capture meaningful paralinguistic structure; straightforward joint modeling without explicit alignment or heuristics
Solid technical execution: methods are sound, training procedures are detailed, and code/models promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (cross-attention, RVQ, Transformer decoders) are established techniques; contribution is primarily their combination for a specific application rather than methodological innovation

Critical ASR dependency not validated: method fundamentally depends on ASR quality but provides no empirical analysis of robustness to ASR errors, domain shifts, or accented speech; a major practical vulnerability
Severely limited experimental scope: English-only evaluation; read speech only (LibriSpeech/LibriTTS); generalization to multilingual, spontaneous, or noisy speech remains unknown

Missing critical ablations: no justification for why last hidden as keys and shallow as values is optimal; no sensitivity analysis on encoder layer selection or RVQ configuration; design choices appear ad-hoc

Duration consistency problem inadequately explained: TASTE has second-worst performance (0.91 vs 0.96-0.98 for others) on duration consistency; dismissive explanation contradicts claims about preserving paralinguistic information
Vocabulary mismatch solution is unprincipled: Algorithm 1 (word-level averaging) works pragmatically but lacks theoretical justification; feels like a workaround rather than principled solution
Computational efficiency not analyzed: no latency/runtime comparison despite acknowledged limitation; critical for practical deployment of SLMs
Moderate human evaluation scale: only 20 samples with 10+ evaluators; heavy reliance on GPT-4o for semantic evaluation risks systematic bias
Comparison fairness issues: different base model sizes (1B vs 7B), S3 baseline surprisingly poor with unclear implementation, cascade comparison uses different architecture
Scope limitations not fully acknowledged: only read speech from controlled datasets; unclear how method handles conversational speech, disfluencies, or speaker variability

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies the mismatch between text and speech tokenization in current joint modeling approaches, providing a concrete problem to address.
Novel and elegant solution: The text-aligned tokenization using cross-attention aggregation is simple, intuitive, and avoids complex external alignment procedures.

Comprehensive evaluation: Extensive experiments across multiple dimensions including speech reconstruction, speech continuation, semantic coherence, likelihood-based evaluation, and downstream tasks with both automatic metrics and human evaluation.
Strong empirical results on downstream tasks: TASLM achieves competitive or superior performance on speech continuation and spoken QA with fewer parameters (1.3B vs 7B+) than baseline SLMs.
Practical applicability demonstrated: Shows concrete applications beyond benchmarks including text-aligned speech editing and few-shot QA capabilities, with code and models promised.
Thorough reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, algorithms (including word-level alignment), and supplementary results in extensive appendices.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Individual components are standard; core insight of using text to guide aggregation is relatively straightforward. The contribution is more engineering-focused than methodologically fundamental.

Significant speech reconstruction quality trade-off: TASTE achieves substantially lower reconstruction quality than alternatives (4.29 vs 1.38 ASR-WER for Encodec; 4.10 vs 3.26 UTMOS). The trade-off justification is insufficient for applications requiring high-fidelity reconstruction.

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation restricted to English; explicitly defers multilingual generalization to future work. Single-speaker focus; multi-speaker scenarios unclear. Limits broader impact.

Insufficient comparison with concurrent joint text-speech methods: Mentions recent work (Défossez et al. 2024, Xie & Wu 2024) doing similar joint modeling but lacks direct experimental comparisons on identical benchmarks.

Evaluation concerns: Human evaluation (MUSHRA) uses only 20 samples; speech continuation evaluation relies on automatic metrics (GPT-4o, UTMOS) with potential biases; no inter-evaluator agreement metrics; limited sample size for strong statistical conclusions.

Alignment quality not thoroughly analyzed: Cross-attention visualizations are qualitative only. No explicit metric for alignment quality. CCA analysis limited to appendix. Unclear if alignment is robustly learned.

Design choice justifications lacking: Limited ablation on architectural decisions (e.g., why shallow Whisper layer?). Weighted sum modality fusion (A.5) appears ad-hoc. RVQ hyperparameters (R=4, 512 codebook) optimality unexplored.

Vocabulary mismatch handling adds complexity: Algorithm 1's word-level grouping and alignment is convoluted, suggesting base alignment insufficient. Information loss risk in this procedure not discussed.

Scalability and efficiency unaddressed: No computational cost, training time, or inference speed comparisons. Method requires both ASR and transcription, adding pipeline complexity. Unclear if benefits justify overhead.

Limited downstream task coverage: Question answering is primarily text continuation rather than true speech understanding. Missing practical tasks (dialogue, translation). QA results show modest improvements with limited baseline coverage.
Presentation issues: Key design choices and loss weightings relegated to appendix. Distinction from concurrent work could be clearer. Algorithm 1 complexity suggests potential robustness issues.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Identifies and addresses the genuine length-mismatch problem in existing speech tokenization methods for joint text-speech modeling
Effective technical solution: Text-aligned attention mechanism is intuitive, well-motivated, and demonstrates clear benefits over alternatives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple complementary metrics (quality, similarity, naturalness), datasets, baselines, and downstream tasks; includes both automatic and human evaluation

Strong empirical results: Competitive speech reconstruction quality with effective joint spoken language modeling; consistent improvements across tasks; outperforms other pre-trained SLMs on benchmarks

Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, evaluation protocols; promises code and model release; extensive supplementary material with ablations and implementation details
Practical applicability: Demonstrates useful capabilities (text-aligned speech editing, few-shot spoken QA) that showcase the framework's utility
Thorough ablation studies: Table 4 clearly shows contribution of each component (encoder, aggregator, quantizer)
Well-organized presentation: Clear motivation, good figures and comprehensive tables, logical flow, and detailed appendices
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: Individual components (standard multi-head attention, RVQ quantization, straightforward architecture) are known techniques; main novelty lies in application rather than algorithmic innovation

ASR dependency and vocabulary mismatch: TASTE requires ASR transcriptions and must handle vocabulary mismatches through word-level grouping/averaging (Appendix A.4), which adds complexity and somewhat undermines the 'direct alignment' claim
Limited experimental scope: Only English language tested; no cross-lingual evaluation; minimal multi-speaker scenario exploration; limits generalizability claims
Modest empirical improvements: While consistent, improvements over baselines are often small (e.g., UtMOS metric differences of 0.02 in Table 1); no statistical significance testing provided
Limited downstream task evaluation: Only two tasks demonstrated (speech continuation, QA); QA results are modest; missing important evaluations on ASR, speaker ID, emotion recognition

Scalability and efficiency questions: Only 1.3B parameter models demonstrated; unclear scalability to larger models (10B+); no training cost comparisons with baselines; attention aggregation computational overhead not analyzed

Incomplete design justification: Necessity of using both text transcription and ASR transcription not well-motivated; choice of Whisper layer depth requires CCA analysis in appendix rather than principled main-text discussion
Missing failure analysis: No systematic analysis of when/where TASTE fails; no exploration across different phonetic contexts, acoustic conditions, or data regimes
